# Lecture 6: Interactions and curvature {#i06} ::: {.outcomes} By the end of Lecture 6, you can - interpret an interaction coefficient as a difference in slopes, also when it is not significant - tell a moderator from a mediator and a confounder - fit a quadratic term and compute a fitted change from the curve - test added terms jointly and avoid using a curve beyond the data ::: ::: {.driving-question} Driving question

An average slope can hide important differences. A relationship may differ between groups, or its slope may change as a predictor grows. Interactions and curved terms let a model show these patterns.

The equity offered (`equity_offered_pct`) in the Shark Tank file falls over the seasons. Is this trend the same for every kind of presenting team, and is it a straight line at all? ::: ::: {.course-phase .phase-before} ## Before class Do all the preparation below before class.
Video preparation
Watch Stanford Statistical Learning 3.5 Extensions of the Linear Model and 7.1 Polynomials and Step Functions. Focus on why an interaction changes a slope, and why a model with a quadratic term (a squared predictor) is still a linear regression. All links are also listed in the External Video Guide. The videos explain key ideas in another way and can use a different notation. The lecture material and its notation always come first.
**Derive the two lines.** In the model $Y=\beta_0+\beta_1X+\beta_2D+\beta_3XD+\varepsilon$ with a dummy variable $D\in\{0,1\}$, write the line for $D=0$ and the line for $D=1$. ::: {.callout-note collapse="true"} ## Check your preparation For $D=0$: $E[Y\mid X,D=0]=\beta_0+\beta_1X$. For $D=1$: $E[Y\mid X,D=1]=(\beta_0+\beta_2)+(\beta_1+\beta_3)X$. Setting $D=1$ shifts the intercept by $\beta_2$ and the slope by $\beta_3$. ::: **Predict.** Answer this question before you come to class: how many separate numbers do you need to fully describe a picture of two straight lines with different slopes? Choose one answer. You will find the answer in the lecture material. [Shark Tank data]{.shark-tag} **R warm-up.** Build the variables for the analysis. The code uses the same `known_gender` subset as Lecture 5: the 1,434 pitches with a known team classification. It adds a dummy `women` and a centred season `season_c`, which is the season minus the mean season. It then fits one line of equity offered on season for each group and draws both lines. Bring the plot: ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} sharks <- read.csv("data/shark_tank_teaching.csv", stringsAsFactors = FALSE) sharks$ask_1k <- sharks$ask_amount_usd / 1000 known_gender <- subset(sharks, pitcher_gender_group != "unknown") known_gender$women <- as.integer( known_gender$pitcher_gender_group %in% c("all_women", "mixed") ) known_gender$season_c <- known_gender$season - mean(known_gender$season) plot(equity_offered_pct ~ season, data = known_gender, pch = 16, col = "grey80") abline(lm(equity_offered_pct ~ season, data = subset(known_gender, women == 0)), col = "#0072B2", lwd = 3) abline(lm(equity_offered_pct ~ season, data = subset(known_gender, women == 1)), col = "#D55E00", lwd = 3) ``` ::: **Code along (bring your laptop).** Bring a charged laptop with RStudio and the course project open. All the code of the lecture is in this chapter, ready to copy. You can run each step yourself during the lecture and get the same numbers and figures. If you are not sure about products, powers, or centring, review [Mathematics Refresher: products, interactions, and combined effects](../resources/math-refresher.html#products-interactions-and-combined-effects) and [polynomial terms](../resources/math-refresher.html#polynomial-terms). ::: ::: {.course-phase .phase-in-class} ## Lecture material This section adds two terms to the regression model. An interaction term lets a slope differ between two groups, or change with the value of another predictor. A quadratic term lets a slope change along the predictor itself.

Stanford explanations (review): 3.5 Extensions of the Linear Model and 7.1 Polynomials and Step Functions.

### Start with a founder's question Does advertising work equally well in every week? Does a trend go on in a straight line forever? Often the answer is "it depends". The two tools of this lecture let you check this in the data. An interaction lets a slope differ between groups. A curve lets a slope change as the predictor grows. ### The picture before the formula In every model so far, all groups had the same slope. Lecture 5 let the height of the line differ between groups. Now the slope may differ as well. Start with the picture in @fig-i06-two-lines: ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code code-fold="true" code-summary="See the R code for this figure"} old_par <- par(no.readonly = TRUE) par(mar = c(4.2, 4.2, 1, 1), las = 1) plot(NA, xlim = c(0, 10), ylim = c(0, 10), bty = "n", xlab = "Predictor X", ylab = "Outcome Y") abline(a = 2, b = 0.75, col = "#009E73", lwd = 3) abline(a = 4.5, b = 0.25, col = "#D55E00", lwd = 3, lty = 2) text(8.4, 2 + 0.75 * 8.4 + 0.9, "Group D = 0", col = "#009E73") text(8.4, 4.5 + 0.25 * 8.4 - 0.8, "Group D = 1", col = "#D55E00") par(old_par) ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} ![Two groups, two lines, different slopes (an invented picture). How many numbers do you need to describe this picture completely?](i06-interactions-curvature_files/figure-html/fig-i06-two-lines-1.png){#fig-i06-two-lines width=672} ::: ::: This answers the prediction question from before class: four numbers, an intercept and a slope for each line. The interaction model writes the same four numbers in a different way: $$ E[Y\mid X,D] =\beta_0+\beta_1X+\beta_2D+\beta_3XD. $$ Each coefficient is one feature of the picture: - $\beta_0$: where the $D=0$ line meets the vertical axis - $\beta_1$: the slope of the $D=0$ line - $\beta_2$: how much higher the $D=1$ line starts - $\beta_3$: how much steeper the $D=1$ line is. The same in a table with one row per group, as you derived it before class: | Group | Intercept | Slope | |---|---|---| | $D=0$ | $\beta_0$ | $\beta_1$ | | $D=1$ | $\beta_0+\beta_2$ | $\beta_1+\beta_3$ | When $\beta_3=0$ the two lines are parallel, and the model is the dummy model of Lecture 5 with one common slope. ### The interaction coefficient is a difference in slopes ::: {.definition-box} Definition **Interaction term.** A term that is the product of two predictors, for example $X\times D$. It lets the slope of one predictor depend on the value of the other. Its coefficient is a difference in slopes. ::: In the additive model the slope of $X$ is the same at every value of the other predictor. With the product $XD$ in the model, a one-unit increase in $X$ changes the conditional mean by $$ \beta_1+\beta_3D. $$ So $\beta_3$ is the difference between the slope of the group with $D=1$ and the slope of the reference category ($D=0$). It is not an effect on its own. Its unit combines the two variables. If $X$ is measured in seasons and $D$ is a dummy, $\beta_3$ is in outcome units per season: here, equity percentage points per season, the group with $D=1$ minus the reference category. The same algebra works when the second variable is a number $Z$ and not a dummy. The slope of $X$ is then $\beta_1+\beta_3Z$, a slope that changes with $Z$. The section on a continuous moderator below works through this case. [**Centring.**]{#i06-centring} Centring a predictor means subtracting its mean. With $XD$ in the model, $\beta_2$ compares the two groups at $X=0$. For the Shark Tank data this would be Season 0, which does not exist. Replacing season with $$ \text{season\_c} = \text{season} - \overline{\text{season}} $$ moves that comparison to the average season (about 8.8). Centring changes some results and cannot change others: - It changes the meaning and the value of the intercept and of the dummy coefficient. Both now refer to the average season. - It cannot change the fitted values, the residuals, $R^2$, or the interaction coefficient. The lines are the same lines. Only the place where we compare the two groups has moved. ::: {.callout-note collapse="true"} ## Check: which printed numbers change when season is centred? The intercept and the `women` coefficient change. The interaction coefficient, the `ask_1k` coefficient, all fitted values, and $R^2$ do not. You will check this in R in the after-class practice. ::: ::: {.callout-caution collapse="true"} ## Try it: two lines from four coefficients Try this with your neighbour first. In an invented example, a venture models weekly orders with advertising spend in euros, a dummy for exam weeks, and their interaction: fitted orders = 100 + 0.10 × ads + 15 × exam + 0.12 × ads × exam. *Step 1 (given).* In ordinary weeks (exam = 0) the line is 100 + 0.10 × ads. *Step 2 (you).* Write the line for exam weeks. *Step 3 (you).* Compare the fitted orders at 200 euros of advertising in the two kinds of weeks, and say what the coefficient 0.12 means. ::: {.callout-note collapse="true"} ## Check your answer Exam weeks: (100 + 15) + (0.10 + 0.12) × ads = 115 + 0.22 × ads. At 200 euros: 120 orders in an ordinary week and 159 in an exam week. The coefficient 0.12 is the difference between the two slopes: each euro of advertising goes with 0.12 more orders in an exam week than in an ordinary week. ::: ::: ### The Shark Tank interaction model [Shark Tank data]{.shark-tag} Now answer the first part of the driving question. In this lecture, `women = 1` means that the presenting team is classified as all-women or mixed, and `women = 0` means all-men. This split is broader than the three categories of Lecture 5. It does not measure the share of women or the full team behind the venture. As before, we leave out the seven `unknown` records. The code first builds the variables, as in the R warm-up: ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} sharks <- read.csv("data/shark_tank_teaching.csv", stringsAsFactors = FALSE) sharks$ask_1k <- sharks$ask_amount_usd / 1000 known_gender <- subset(sharks, pitcher_gender_group != "unknown") known_gender$women <- as.integer( known_gender$pitcher_gender_group %in% c("all_women", "mixed") ) known_gender$season_c <- known_gender$season - mean(known_gender$season) interaction_model <- lm( equity_offered_pct ~ season_c * women + ask_1k, data = known_gender ) summary(interaction_model) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` Call: lm(formula = equity_offered_pct ~ season_c * women + ask_1k, data = known_gender) Residuals: Min 1Q Median 3Q Max -15.871 -4.742 -1.290 3.412 82.689 Coefficients: Estimate Std. Error t value Pr(>|t|) (Intercept) 13.6247907 0.3354522 40.616 < 2e-16 *** season_c -0.7993817 0.0663226 -12.053 < 2e-16 *** women 0.8069665 0.4117061 1.960 0.0502 . ask_1k -0.0026776 0.0005834 -4.590 4.83e-06 *** season_c:women -0.0614594 0.0955667 -0.643 0.5203 --- Signif. codes: 0 '***' 0.001 '**' 0.01 '*' 0.05 '.' 0.1 ' ' 1 Residual standard error: 7.62 on 1429 degrees of freedom Multiple R-squared: 0.1894, Adjusted R-squared: 0.1871 F-statistic: 83.47 on 4 and 1429 DF, p-value: < 2.2e-16 ``` ::: ::: ::: {#exm-i06-reading-interaction} ## Worked example: reading each coefficient of the interaction model [Shark Tank data]{.shark-tag} The outcome is the equity offered in percent, so every coefficient is in percentage points. The predictor `season_c` is in seasons, measured from the average season. The requested amount `ask_1k` is in \$1,000s. The reference category is all-men teams (`women = 0`). The code below stores the coefficients and computes the two group lines at the average requested amount: ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} b_int <- coef(interaction_model) ask_bar <- mean(known_gender$ask_1k) intercept_men <- unname(b_int["(Intercept)"] + b_int["ask_1k"] * ask_bar) intercept_women <- intercept_men + unname(b_int["women"]) c(intercept_men = intercept_men, intercept_women = intercept_women, slope_men = unname(b_int["season_c"]), slope_women = unname(b_int["season_c"] + b_int["season_c:women"])) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` intercept_men intercept_women slope_men slope_women 12.8661626 13.6731291 -0.7993817 -0.8608411 ``` ::: ```{.r .cell-code} c(mean_season = mean(known_gender$season), min_ask_1k = min(known_gender$ask_1k), gap_share_of_men = unname(b_int["women"]) / intercept_men, interaction_share_of_slope = unname(b_int["season_c:women"] / b_int["season_c"])) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` mean_season min_ask_1k 8.77894003 10.00000000 gap_share_of_men interaction_share_of_slope 0.06272006 0.07688369 ``` ::: ::: Step 1: the two lines. Fill in the table with one row per group. At the average requested amount, with $\text{season\_c}$ as the predictor: $$ \begin{aligned} \text{all-men teams: } & \widehat{\text{equity}} = 12.866 - 0.799\times\text{season\_c},\\ \text{teams with women: } & \widehat{\text{equity}} = (12.866+0.807) + (-0.7994-0.0615)\times\text{season\_c}\\ & \phantom{\widehat{\text{equity}}} = 13.673 - 0.861\times\text{season\_c}. \end{aligned} $$ Step 2: one sentence per coefficient. - `season_c` ($-0.799$). Among all-men teams, one season later is associated with an equity offered that is on average 0.80 percentage points lower, at the same requested amount. This is the slope of the reference category only. - `season_c:women` ($-0.061$). Per one season more, the equity offered by teams with women falls 0.061 percentage points more than that of all-men teams. This is the difference between the two slopes. It is about 8% of the all-men slope. - `women` ($0.807$). In the average season (about 8.8), teams with women are fitted to offer about 0.81 percentage points more equity than all-men teams, at the same requested amount. With the interaction in the model, this difference holds only where $\text{season\_c}=0$. In other seasons the gap is $0.807-0.061\times\text{season\_c}$. - `ask_1k` ($-0.0027$). A request that is \$1,000 higher is associated with an equity offered that is on average 0.0027 percentage points lower, in both groups. Per \$100,000 more, this is about 0.27 percentage points. - The intercept ($13.62$) is the fitted equity offered for all-men teams in the average season with a requested amount of \$0. The smallest request in the data is \$10,000, so the intercept has no useful meaning of its own. Step 3: how large is it? In the average season, all-men teams are fitted to offer 12.87% and teams with women 13.67%. The gap is 0.81 percentage points. Measured as a percent of the all-men level, the same gap is about 6%. So "0.81 percent more" would be wrong. The coefficient is a difference in percentage points. Why does the model use `season_c` and not `season`? The dummy coefficient always compares the groups at $X=0$. Without [centring](#i06-centring), $X=0$ would be Season 0, a season outside the data. Centring moves the comparison to the average season, where there are many pitches. ::: The interaction estimate is $-0.061$ equity percentage points per season, with a p-value of about 0.520. The difference is small, about 8% of the all-men slope (@exm-i06-reading-interaction). Draw two conclusions from this result. First, the model gives no evidence that the season trend differs between the two groups. Second, the model does not prove that the two slopes are equal. The estimate is imprecise (standard error about 0.096), so the data are consistent with a somewhat steeper trend and also with a somewhat flatter trend for teams with women. No evidence of a difference is not proof of no difference. ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code code-fold="true" code-summary="See the R code for this figure"} library(ggplot2) sharks <- read.csv("data/shark_tank_teaching.csv", stringsAsFactors = FALSE) sharks$ask_1k <- sharks$ask_amount_usd / 1000 known_gender <- subset(sharks, pitcher_gender_group != "unknown") known_gender$women <- as.integer( known_gender$pitcher_gender_group %in% c("all_women", "mixed") ) known_gender$season_c <- known_gender$season - mean(known_gender$season) interaction_model <- lm( equity_offered_pct ~ season_c * women + ask_1k, data = known_gender ) season_grid <- 1:16 ask_bar <- mean(known_gender$ask_1k) newdat <- expand.grid(season = season_grid, women = c(0, 1)) newdat$season_c <- newdat$season - mean(known_gender$season) newdat$ask_1k <- ask_bar newdat$fit <- predict(interaction_model, newdata = newdat) newdat$group <- ifelse(newdat$women == 1, "Teams with women", "All-men") fit_men_13 <- newdat$fit[newdat$women == 0 & newdat$season == 13] fit_women_13 <- newdat$fit[newdat$women == 1 & newdat$season == 13] ggplot(newdat, aes(x = season, y = fit, colour = group, linetype = group)) + geom_line(linewidth = 1.1) + geom_point(data = subset(newdat, season %in% c(1, 16)), size = 2.2) + annotate("text", x = 13, y = fit_women_13 + 1.1, label = "Teams with women", colour = "#D55E00", size = 3.4) + annotate("text", x = 13, y = fit_men_13 - 1.1, label = "All-men", colour = "#009E73", size = 3.4) + scale_colour_manual(values = c("All-men" = "#009E73", "Teams with women" = "#D55E00"), guide = "none") + scale_linetype_manual(values = c("All-men" = "solid", "Teams with women" = "dashed"), guide = "none") + scale_x_continuous(breaks = seq(1, 16, by = 3)) + labs(x = "Season", y = "Fitted initial equity offered (%)") + theme_minimal(base_size = 13) + theme( panel.grid.minor = element_blank(), panel.grid.major.x = element_blank(), plot.caption = element_text(colour = "#5B6976"), axis.title = element_text(colour = "#17324D") ) ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} ![Fitted equity offered by season for all-men teams and for teams with women, at the average requested amount. The two lines are almost parallel. The slope of a line is the fitted change per season for that group, and the vertical distance between the lines is the fitted difference between the groups in a given season.](i06-interactions-curvature_files/figure-html/fig-i06-interaction-1.png){#fig-i06-interaction width=672} ::: ::: Always graph a model that contains an interaction. In @fig-i06-interaction, the main result is that the two lines are almost parallel. Once $XD$ is in the model, neither $\hat\beta_1$ nor $\hat\beta_2$ alone describes all teams. ### A continuous moderator The second variable of an interaction need not be a dummy. It can be any number $Z$, such as a price, a firm size, or a number of stores. The model is $$ E[Y\mid X,Z]=\beta_0+\beta_1X+\beta_2Z+\beta_3XZ, $$ and a one-unit increase in $X$ changes the conditional mean by $\beta_1+\beta_3Z$. There are now not two lines but one line for every value of $Z$. ::: {.definition-box} Definition **Moderator.** A variable $Z$ that changes the slope of another predictor $X$ through the interaction term $XZ$. The slope of $X$ at one value of $Z$, $\beta_1+\beta_3Z$, is called the conditional effect of $X$ at that value. ::: The name "conditional effect" is standard, but it is still a fitted slope. It is a causal effect only when the design of the study allows a causal reading. Two coefficients now need care. $\beta_1$ is the slope of $X$ only where $Z=0$, and $\beta_2$ is the slope of $Z$ only where $X=0$. If zero lies outside the data, neither number describes any real case. The coefficients $\beta_1$ and $\beta_2$ are often called the main effects. With $XZ$ in the model they are conditional too. [Centring](#i06-centring) $Z$ makes $\beta_1$ the slope of $X$ at the mean of $Z$. ::: {#exm-i06-moderator} ## Worked example: marketing pays more in regions with more stores An invented example. A franchise chain has 150 regions. For each region it records the monthly sales and the monthly marketing spending, both in €1,000s, and the number of stores. The question: does an extra €1,000 of marketing go with more sales in regions with many stores? The code below builds the invented data and fits the model with the interaction term: ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} set.seed(606) n_regions <- 150 stores <- sample(1:12, n_regions, replace = TRUE) marketing <- round(runif(n_regions, min = 2, max = 20), 1) sales <- round(30 + 1.0 * marketing + 6 * stores + 0.25 * marketing * stores + rnorm(n_regions, sd = 12), 1) franchise <- data.frame(sales, marketing, stores) summary(franchise) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` sales marketing stores Min. : 32.00 Min. : 2.300 Min. : 1.000 1st Qu.: 72.20 1st Qu.: 6.825 1st Qu.: 3.000 Median : 94.55 Median :11.900 Median : 6.000 Mean : 98.11 Mean :11.487 Mean : 6.313 3rd Qu.:122.20 3rd Qu.:16.300 3rd Qu.:10.000 Max. :198.90 Max. :19.900 Max. :12.000 ``` ::: ```{.r .cell-code} moderator_model <- lm(sales ~ marketing * stores, data = franchise) summary(moderator_model)$coefficients ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` Estimate Std. Error t value Pr(>|t|) (Intercept) 24.9309191 5.04357562 4.943104 2.083727e-06 marketing 1.7446662 0.39007324 4.472663 1.542400e-05 stores 6.7676103 0.68626060 9.861575 6.754837e-18 marketing:stores 0.1474736 0.05500072 2.681304 8.177947e-03 ``` ::: ::: Step 1: the slope of marketing as a function of stores. With the coefficients from the output, $$ \widehat{\text{slope of marketing}} = 1.745 + 0.147\times\text{stores}. $$ Step 2: the slope at three meaningful values of the moderator. Take the lower quartile, the median, and the upper quartile of the number of stores: ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} b_mod <- coef(moderator_model) store_values <- quantile(franchise$stores, c(0.25, 0.5, 0.75)) store_values ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` 25% 50% 75% 3 6 10 ``` ::: ```{.r .cell-code} marketing_slopes <- b_mod["marketing"] + b_mod["marketing:stores"] * store_values marketing_slopes ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` 25% 50% 75% 2.187087 2.629508 3.219403 ``` ::: ```{.r .cell-code} marketing_slopes[3] / marketing_slopes[1] ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` 75% 1.472005 ``` ::: ::: In a region with 3 stores (the lower quartile), €1,000 more marketing is associated with about €2,190 more monthly sales on average. With 6 stores (the median) it is about €2,630, and with 10 stores (the upper quartile) about €3,220. The slope at the upper quartile is about 1.47 times the slope at the lower quartile. Step 3: one sentence per coefficient. - `marketing:stores` ($0.147$). A region with one more store has a marketing slope that is 0.147 higher: €147 more monthly sales per €1,000 of marketing. Read the other way round, a region that spends €1,000 more on marketing has a stores slope that is €147 per store higher. - `marketing` ($1.745$). This is the slope of marketing in a region with 0 stores. No region has 0 stores (the minimum is 1), so this number does not describe the marketing slope of any region. - `stores` ($6.768$). This is the slope of stores at €0 of marketing. The smallest spending in the data is €2,300, so this number also lies outside the data. Step 4: centre the moderator. With $\text{stores\_c}$, the number of stores minus its mean, the marketing coefficient becomes the slope at the average number of stores (about 6.3): ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} franchise$stores_c <- franchise$stores - mean(franchise$stores) coef(lm(sales ~ marketing * stores_c, data = franchise)) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` (Intercept) marketing stores_c marketing:stores_c 67.6570986 2.6757165 6.7676103 0.1474736 ``` ::: ::: The marketing coefficient is now 2.676: at the average number of stores, €1,000 more marketing is associated with about €2,680 more monthly sales. The interaction coefficient stays 0.147. As with the dummy, centring moves the place of the comparison and not the fitted lines. ::: @fig-i06-moderator draws the fitted lines at the three values of the moderator. The lines fan out because their slopes differ. ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code code-fold="true" code-summary="See the R code for this figure"} library(ggplot2) set.seed(606) n_regions <- 150 stores <- sample(1:12, n_regions, replace = TRUE) marketing <- round(runif(n_regions, min = 2, max = 20), 1) sales <- round(30 + 1.0 * marketing + 6 * stores + 0.25 * marketing * stores + rnorm(n_regions, sd = 12), 1) franchise <- data.frame(sales, marketing, stores) moderator_model <- lm(sales ~ marketing * stores, data = franchise) lines_data <- expand.grid(marketing = seq(2, 20, length.out = 50), stores = c(3, 6, 10)) lines_data$fit <- predict(moderator_model, newdata = lines_data) lines_data$group <- factor(paste(lines_data$stores, "stores"), levels = c("3 stores", "6 stores", "10 stores")) label_data <- subset(lines_data, marketing == 20) ggplot(franchise, aes(x = marketing, y = sales)) + geom_point(colour = "grey80", size = 1.6) + geom_line(data = lines_data, aes(x = marketing, y = fit, colour = group, linetype = group), linewidth = 1.1) + geom_text(data = label_data, aes(x = marketing + 0.4, y = fit, label = group, colour = group), hjust = 0, size = 3.4) + scale_colour_manual(values = c("3 stores" = "#009E73", "6 stores" = "#0072B2", "10 stores" = "#D55E00"), guide = "none") + scale_linetype_manual(values = c("3 stores" = "solid", "6 stores" = "longdash", "10 stores" = "dashed"), guide = "none") + coord_cartesian(xlim = c(2, 23)) + labs(x = "Monthly marketing spending (EUR 1,000s)", y = "Monthly sales (EUR 1,000s)") + theme_minimal(base_size = 13) + theme( panel.grid.minor = element_blank(), panel.grid.major.x = element_blank(), plot.caption = element_text(colour = "#5B6976"), axis.title = element_text(colour = "#17324D") ) ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} ![Fitted monthly sales against marketing spending (invented example) in regions with 3, 6, and 10 stores, the quartiles of the number of stores. The lines become steeper as the number of stores grows: the slope of marketing depends on the moderator.](i06-interactions-curvature_files/figure-html/fig-i06-moderator-1.png){#fig-i06-moderator width=672} ::: ::: ### The hierarchy principle and the `*` shorthand The **hierarchy principle** says: if a model contains $XD$, keep both $X$ and $D$ in the model, even when one of them is not significant on its own. The same holds for $XZ$ with a continuous moderator $Z$. The terms $X$ and $D$ define the two lines, and the interaction describes the difference between these lines. If you leave out $D$, the model forces both lines to start at the same height. This distorts the interaction coefficient. The `*` shorthand in an R formula follows the principle for you: ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} lm(y ~ x * z, data = df) # x * z expands to x + z + x:z ``` ::: ### Moderation and mediation Two words often appear in business research about a third variable: a moderator and a mediator. They describe different roles, and a regression handles them in different ways. Moderation first. A moderator changes the strength or the direction of the relationship between $X$ and $Y$. With a moderator, the answer to "how is $X$ related to $Y$?" is "it depends on $Z$". In a regression, moderation shows up as an interaction term. You have seen two cases. In @exm-i06-reading-interaction the moderator is a dummy, the `women` group, and the season slope differs between two groups. In @exm-i06-moderator the moderator is a number, the number of stores, and the marketing slope grows with every extra store. A moderator can also reverse a relationship, for example a price cut that raises orders for students and lowers them for a luxury segment. ::: {.definition-box} Definition **Mediator.** A variable $M$ that lies on the path from $X$ to $Y$: $X$ affects $M$, and $M$ affects $Y$. The part of the effect of $X$ on $Y$ that runs through $M$ is called the indirect effect. ::: Take marketing spending ($X$), website visits ($M$), and sales ($Y$). Marketing brings visitors to the website, and visitors buy. Marketing can also raise sales in other ways, for example through people who see an advert and buy in a shop. @fig-i06-mediation shows the two paths. Three effects describe them: - the total effect: how much $Y$ changes when $X$ changes, by all paths together - the direct effect: the part that does not run through $M$ - the indirect effect: the part that runs through $M$. The total effect is the direct effect plus the indirect effect. ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code code-fold="true" code-summary="See the R code for this figure"} library(ggplot2) boxes <- data.frame(x = c(1, 3, 5), y = c(1, 2, 1), label = c("Marketing\nspending (X)", "Website\nvisits (M)", "Sales (Y)")) arrows_data <- data.frame(x = c(1.45, 3.55, 1.6), y = c(1.25, 1.75, 1), xend = c(2.45, 4.55, 4.4), yend = c(1.75, 1.25, 1), path = c("indirect", "indirect", "direct")) ggplot() + geom_segment(data = arrows_data, aes(x = x, y = y, xend = xend, yend = yend, colour = path), linewidth = 1.1, arrow = arrow(length = grid::unit(0.25, "cm"), type = "closed")) + geom_label(data = boxes, aes(x = x, y = y, label = label), colour = "#17324D", size = 3.6, label.padding = grid::unit(0.4, "lines")) + annotate("text", x = 3, y = 1.55, label = "indirect path", colour = "#009E73", size = 3.4) + annotate("text", x = 3, y = 0.85, label = "direct path", colour = "#D55E00", size = 3.4) + scale_colour_manual(values = c("indirect" = "#009E73", "direct" = "#D55E00"), guide = "none") + coord_cartesian(xlim = c(0.4, 5.6), ylim = c(0.7, 2.3)) + theme_void() ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} ![A mediation diagram (invented example). The indirect path runs from marketing spending through website visits to sales. The direct path goes from marketing spending to sales without visits. The total effect is the sum of both paths.](i06-interactions-curvature_files/figure-html/fig-i06-mediation-1.png){#fig-i06-mediation width=672} ::: ::: ::: {#exm-i06-mediation} ## Worked example: how much of the marketing slope runs through visits? An invented example. For 120 small web shops we know the monthly marketing spending and the monthly sales, both in €1,000s, and the monthly website visits in 1,000s. The code below builds the invented data. It sets a direct path and a path through visits, which a real founder never knows. ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} set.seed(616) n_shops <- 120 marketing <- round(runif(n_shops, min = 2, max = 12), 1) visits <- round(4 + 1.5 * marketing + rnorm(n_shops, sd = 2), 1) sales <- round(20 + 2 * marketing + 2 * visits + rnorm(n_shops, sd = 5), 1) shop <- data.frame(sales, marketing, visits) total_model <- lm(sales ~ marketing, data = shop) direct_model <- lm(sales ~ marketing + visits, data = shop) visits_model <- lm(visits ~ marketing, data = shop) coef(total_model) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` (Intercept) marketing 28.613248 5.039895 ``` ::: ```{.r .cell-code} coef(direct_model) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` (Intercept) marketing visits 21.194789 2.621621 1.625205 ``` ::: ```{.r .cell-code} coef(visits_model) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` (Intercept) marketing 4.564631 1.487982 ``` ::: ```{.r .cell-code} total <- unname(coef(total_model)["marketing"]) direct <- unname(coef(direct_model)["marketing"]) c(total = total, direct = direct, through_visits = total - direct, share_through_visits = (total - direct) / total) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` total direct through_visits 5.0398953 2.6216208 2.4182745 share_through_visits 0.4798263 ``` ::: ```{.r .cell-code} unname(coef(visits_model)["marketing"] * coef(direct_model)["visits"]) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` [1] 2.418274 ``` ::: ::: Step 1: the total association. Without visits in the model, €1,000 more marketing is associated with about €5,040 more monthly sales on average. Step 2: the direct part. With visits added, the marketing coefficient falls to 2.62. At the same number of visits, €1,000 more marketing is associated with about €2,620 more sales. Step 3: the part through visits. The difference is $5.04-2.62=2.42$, about €2,420 of sales per €1,000 of marketing. That is about 48% of the total. The same number comes from the two paths. €1,000 more marketing goes with about 1,490 more visits ($1.488$ in 1,000s), and 1,000 more visits go with about €1,630 more sales at the same marketing ($1.625$). The product is $1.488\times1.625\approx2.42$. ::: A mediator is not a control variable. In [Lecture 4](i04-multiple-regression.qmd#what-control-variables-can-and-cannot-do) you added control variables to hold confounders fixed. A mediator looks like one more predictor, but adding it changes the question. With visits in the model, the marketing coefficient no longer contains the part that runs through visits. If you want the total effect of marketing, do not control for visits. So ask first what role a variable plays. Control for a confounder. Do not control for a mediator when you want the total effect. Mediation is a causal idea. It needs a causal design, such as an experiment, or strong assumptions. With observational data, the split into a direct and an indirect part only describes the data. The table compares the three roles of a third variable $Z$. | Role | What it is | How it appears in a regression | Example | |---|---|---|---| | Moderator | Changes the slope of $X$ | Interaction term $XZ$ | Number of stores changes the marketing slope | | Mediator | Lies on the path from $X$ to $Y$ | Adding it shrinks the coefficient of $X$ to the direct part | Website visits between marketing and sales | | Confounder | Affects both $X$ and $Y$ | Control variable, to remove omitted variable bias | Firm size behind both advertising and sales | ### Curvature: polynomials are still linear regression An interaction term lets the slope of $x$ differ by group or change with a moderator. A quadratic term, defined below, lets the slope change as $x$ itself changes. Both add one new column to the data, a product or a square. In both, you read two coefficients together. [Shark Tank data]{.shark-tag} Is the season trend a straight line at all? To let it bend, add the square of the predictor. ::: {.definition-box} Definition **Quadratic term.** The square of a predictor, $x^2$, added to a model that also contains $x$. It lets the fitted line bend, so the slope changes with $x$. A model with powers of a predictor is called a polynomial. ::: The quadratic conditional mean $$ E[Y\mid X=x]=\beta_0+\beta_1x+\beta_2x^2 $$ is curved in $x$, but it is linear in the unknown coefficients $\beta_0,\beta_1,\beta_2$. Linearity in the coefficients is all that `lm()` requires. The square is one more column of data. What changes is how you read the output. The slope is no longer one number. Moving from $x$ to $x+1$ changes the conditional mean by $$ (\beta_1(x+1)+\beta_2(x+1)^2) - (\beta_1x+\beta_2x^2) =\beta_1+\beta_2(2x+1). $$ This change depends on the starting value $x$. The rule is: never read $\beta_1$ alone while $x^2$ is in the model. Calculate fitted changes or graph the curve. ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} linear_season <- lm(equity_offered_pct ~ season + ask_1k, data = sharks) poly_season <- lm(equity_offered_pct ~ season + I(season^2) + ask_1k, data = sharks) summary(poly_season)$coefficients ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` Estimate Std. Error t value Pr(>|t|) (Intercept) 24.171680818 0.8205664983 29.457309 1.332051e-149 season -1.713233277 0.2056686354 -8.330066 1.862369e-16 I(season^2) 0.051034200 0.0113694269 4.488722 7.737227e-06 ask_1k -0.002710806 0.0005740121 -4.722559 2.556506e-06 ``` ::: ::: `I()` tells R to calculate the square. Without `I()`, R would read `^` as part of the formula syntax and not as a square. The fitted coefficients are $\hat\beta_1 \approx -1.713$ for `season` and $\hat\beta_2 \approx 0.051$ for `I(season^2)`. Together they describe a steep decline in the early seasons that becomes flatter season by season. ::: {#exm-i06-quadratic-change} ## Worked example: the fitted change from Season 5 to Season 6 [Shark Tank data]{.shark-tag} Holding requested amount fixed, the fitted change from season $x$ to season $x+1$ is $\hat\beta_1+\hat\beta_2(2x+1)$. From Season 5 to Season 6, $x = 5$: $$ \hat\beta_1+\hat\beta_2(2\times5+1) =-1.713+0.051\times11 =-1.713+0.561 \approx-1.15 \text{ percentage points.} $$ Reading $\hat\beta_1=-1.713$ alone would make the drop about 0.56 points too large, which is about half of the fitted drop of 1.15 points. The number $-1.713$ is not a constant slope. It describes the slope at $x=0$, a season that does not exist. Check the calculation in R with the stored coefficients: ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} b <- coef(poly_season) unname(b["season"] + b["I(season^2)"] * (2 * 5 + 1)) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` [1] -1.151857 ``` ::: ::: ::: ### Is the curvature worth having? The partial F [Shark Tank data]{.shark-tag} The quadratic model and the linear model are nested, so the partial F-test of Lecture 5 applies to the one added term: ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} anova(linear_season, poly_season) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` Analysis of Variance Table Model 1: equity_offered_pct ~ season + ask_1k Model 2: equity_offered_pct ~ season + I(season^2) + ask_1k Res.Df RSS Df Sum of Sq F Pr(>F) 1 1438 83493 2 1437 82338 1 1154.5 20.149 7.737e-06 *** --- Signif. codes: 0 '***' 0.001 '**' 0.01 '*' 0.05 '.' 0.1 ' ' 1 ``` ::: ::: The partial F-test for adding `I(season^2)` gives $F \approx 20.1$ with a p-value below 0.001. The data show a curve. But the gain in fit is small: adjusted $R^2$ rises from about 0.186 to about 0.196, one percentage point more of the variation in the equity offered. So also look at the shape of the curve in @fig-i06-polynomial: ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code code-fold="true" code-summary="See the R code for this figure"} library(ggplot2) sharks <- read.csv("data/shark_tank_teaching.csv", stringsAsFactors = FALSE) sharks$ask_1k <- sharks$ask_amount_usd / 1000 poly_season <- lm(equity_offered_pct ~ season + I(season^2) + ask_1k, data = sharks) season_means <- aggregate(equity_offered_pct ~ season, data = sharks, mean) curve_data <- data.frame(season = seq(1, 16, length.out = 200), ask_1k = mean(sharks$ask_1k)) curve_data$fit <- predict(poly_season, newdata = curve_data) ggplot(season_means, aes(x = season, y = equity_offered_pct)) + annotate("rect", xmin = 16, xmax = 17.6, ymin = -Inf, ymax = Inf, fill = "grey75", alpha = 0.25) + geom_vline(xintercept = 16, colour = "grey60", linetype = "dashed", linewidth = 0.8) + geom_line(data = curve_data, aes(x = season, y = fit), colour = "#D55E00", linewidth = 1.1) + geom_point(size = 2.6, colour = "#009E73") + annotate("text", x = 16.8, y = max(season_means$equity_offered_pct), label = "no data beyond\nseason 16", colour = "#5B6976", size = 3, lineheight = 0.95) + scale_x_continuous(breaks = seq(1, 16, by = 3)) + coord_cartesian(xlim = c(1, 17.6)) + labs(x = "Season", y = "Initial equity offered (%)") + theme_minimal(base_size = 13) + theme( panel.grid.minor = element_blank(), panel.grid.major.x = element_blank(), plot.caption = element_text(colour = "#5B6976"), axis.title = element_text(colour = "#17324D") ) ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} ![Season means of the equity offered (points) and the fitted quadratic curve at the average requested amount. The curve becomes flatter towards the last observed seasons. Beyond Season 16 (shaded) it would turn upward, but there are no data in that region.](i06-interactions-curvature_files/figure-html/fig-i06-polynomial-1.png){#fig-i06-polynomial width=672} ::: ::: The points in @fig-i06-polynomial are the plain means of each season. The curve keeps the requested amount fixed at its sample mean. To extrapolate means to use a fitted model outside the range of the data. Do not extrapolate the quadratic beyond Seasons 1--16. The fitted curve reaches its lowest point just after Season 16 and would rise steeply afterwards. This rise comes from the shape of a quadratic, not from any data, so it is not a forecast. ::: {.caveat-box} What flexible terms can and cannot repair - Interactions and curves make the model more flexible. They cannot fix problems in how the data were produced. - Every added term costs precision. Add a term because your question needs it, not because it turns out to be significant. - You can trust a curve only inside the range of the data. **What you can do with it:** ask whether a relationship could differ between groups or follow a curve, add that one term, graph the fitted lines, and report combined results. ::: ### Answering the driving question **The same trend for every kind of team?** The estimated difference in slopes is $-0.061$ percentage points per season (p $\approx$ 0.52). The data show no difference between all-men teams and teams with women. They also do not prove that the trends are equal, because the estimate is imprecise. **A straight line?** Not quite. The quadratic term is significant (partial $F \approx 20.1$, p $<$ 0.001). The fitted decline becomes flatter: from about $-1.56$ points per season between Seasons 1 and 2 to about $-0.64$ between Seasons 10 and 11. Use the curve only inside Seasons 1--16. The founder's questions at the start of the lecture get the same two kinds of answer. Whether advertising works equally well in every week is a question about an interaction. In the invented example of the Try it task, advertising does not work equally well: the slope is 0.10 orders per euro in ordinary weeks and 0.22 in exam weeks. Whether a trend goes on in a straight line is a question about a curve. The season trend of the equity offered does not go on in a straight line: the fitted drop per season shrinks from about 1.56 to about 0.64 points, and beyond Season 16 the data say nothing. ::: {.founder-box} A founder's decision (invented example) You suspect that advertising works better in exam weeks. The model with an interaction gives an advertising slope of 0.10 orders per euro in ordinary weeks and 0.10 + 0.12 = 0.22 in exam weeks. After a price increase, each order now brings 6 euros of margin. So 100 euros of advertising goes with 10 more orders and 60 euros of margin in an ordinary week, which is less than the advertising costs. In an exam week it goes with 22 more orders and 132 euros of margin. The decision: advertise in the exam weeks only. One check first: the interaction of 0.12 has its own interval. If that interval includes zero, the data do not yet show that the two kinds of weeks differ. Then keep spreading the advertising budget over both kinds of weeks for one more study period before you decide. ::: **Next:** Tutorial 2 practises Lectures 4--6 with exam-style questions. It ends with one full analysis, from a research question to a conclusion of 150 words. Your thesis asks for this kind of analysis too. ::: ::: {.course-phase .phase-after} ## After class After the lecture, work through all the practice below. ### Read the lecture material Read the Lecture material section above from start to end. So that the intercept and the dummy coefficient refer to a useful value, such as the sample mean, and not to zero. Centring moved the place where we compare the two groups. It did not move the lines. ::: ### Finish a half-worked example: a quadratic change [Shark Tank data]{.shark-tag} Read the worked calculation for Season 5 to Season 6 again (@exm-i06-quadratic-change). A large p-value means the data do not show a difference. It does not prove that the trends are the same, because the estimate is imprecise. And with an interaction in the model, -0.80 is the trend for the group coded 0, the all-men teams. For teams with women it is -0.80 - 0.06 = -0.86. ::: ### Make it yours :::: {.utility-prompt} Two sentences about your own venture Think of your EiA3 venture, or any business you know well. Name one relationship in its data whose slope could depend on something else. For example, the response to price may differ by customer segment, the result of a campaign may differ by channel, or growth may become flatter as the business gets larger. Then write two sentences. First, state the interaction or quadratic term you would add and the question behind it. Second, say what a result that is not significant would tell you, and what it would not tell you.
